Credit reporting or credit repair: Credit reports and scores from credit bureaus or other consumer reporting companies (such as tenant or check-writing screening): their accuracy, disputes and use, plus credit repair, credit monitoring and identity theft protection services.
Debt collection: Efforts by a collector, debt buyer or creditor to collect a debt the consumer allegedly owes, including collection calls, letters, lawsuits and disputes that the debt is owed.
Mortgage: A home loan or home equity loan: applying, refinancing, closing, paying the servicer, escrow, loan modification, foreclosure or other problems with the mortgage itself.
Credit card or prepaid card: A credit card, store card, charge card or prepaid card (including gift, payroll and government benefit cards): purchases, fees, payments, rewards, getting or closing the card.
Checking or savings account: A bank or credit union deposit account such as checking, savings or a CD: opening, managing or closing it, deposits and withdrawals, overdrafts, holds and account fees.
Student loan: A federal or private loan taken out to pay for education: getting the loan, dealing with the servicer, repayment plans, forgiveness, deferment or struggling to repay.
Vehicle loan or lease: Financing or leasing a car or other vehicle: getting the loan or lease, payments, repossession, and problems at the end of the loan or lease.
Money transfer, virtual currency, or mon: Sending or receiving money through a transfer service or payment app, mobile wallets, cryptocurrency, money orders, check cashing, or foreign currency exchange.
Payday, title, or personal loan: A payday loan, vehicle title loan, pawn loan, installment or personal loan, or personal line of credit that is not a mortgage, vehicle, or student loan.
Attempts to collect debt not owed: The consumer says the debt being collected is not theirs, was already paid, came from identity theft, or was discharged in bankruptcy. A dispute only about the amount belongs to false statements.
Written notification about debt: The collector did not send enough written information to verify the debt, did not give notice of the right to dispute, or did not disclose that it was trying to collect a debt.
Took or threatened to take negative or l: The collector threatened to damage the consumer's credit, sued or threatened to sue (including over very old debt, without proper notice or in the wrong state), seized property or exempt funds, or threatened arrest or deportation.
False statements or representation: The collector tried to collect the wrong amount, impersonated an attorney, police or government official, said not paying is a crime, or told the consumer not to respond to a lawsuit.
Communication tactics: How the collector contacts the consumer: frequent or repeated calls, calls before 8am or after 9pm, abusive or profane language, or continuing to contact the consumer after being told to stop.
Threatened to contact someone or share i: The collector talked to a third party such as family, friends or the employer about the debt, contacted the employer, or contacted the consumer directly instead of their attorney.
Trouble during payment process: Problems while repaying an existing mortgage: payments not credited or misapplied, escrow, taxes and insurance, fees, servicing transfers, statements or payoff issues.
Struggling to pay mortgage: The borrower cannot keep up with payments: loan modification, forbearance, short sale, foreclosure or other help for a mortgage in trouble.
Applying for a mortgage or refinancing a: Problems while applying for a new mortgage or a refinance: the application process, credit decision, rates, terms or delays before closing.
Closing on a mortgage: Problems at the closing stage of a mortgage: closing costs, changed terms, disclosures, delays, or documents at or around settlement.
Managing an account: Problems with an open account's everyday use: deposits and withdrawals, funds not handled as instructed, banking errors, debit or ATM card problems, account access, fees, payments or cashing a check.
Closing an account: The bank closed the account, the consumer could not close it, funds from the closed account were not received, or fees were charged for closing it.
Opening an account: Problems opening a deposit account: being unable to open one, an account opened through fraud, advertised terms or bonuses not received, or confusing or missing disclosures.
Problem with a lender or other company c: Another company or lender debited the account without authorization, took the wrong amount, or kept charging after being told to stop.
Problem caused by your funds being low: Overdraft or insufficient-funds fees, bounced or returned payments, overdraft coverage, or other problems because the account balance was too low.
Incorrect information on your report: The report itself is wrong: information belongs to someone else, account status or details are wrong, personal or public-record information is wrong, old items reappear, or information is missing. Choose this when the complaint is mainly about the errors, not about a dispute being mishandled.
Problem with a credit reporting company': The consumer already disputed with the reporting company and the dispute handling failed: the investigation did not fix the error, took over 30 days, results were never sent, the dispute was hard to submit, or the statement of dispute was mishandled.
Improper use of your report: The report was used or shared without permission: inquiries the consumer does not recognise, the reporting company using the report improperly, a report given to an employer without consent, or offers received after opting out.
Unable to get your credit report or cred: The consumer could not obtain their credit report or score, including the free annual credit report, for example because identity verification failed or requests were ignored.
Problem with fraud alerts or security fr: Problems placing, lifting or keeping a fraud alert or security freeze on the credit file, or the freeze or alert not working as it should.
Credit monitoring or identity theft prot: Problems with paid credit monitoring or identity theft protection products: billing disputes, trouble cancelling, services not delivered as advertised, terms changing, or unwanted marketing.
Managing the loan or lease: Problems during an existing vehicle loan or lease: billing problems, fees charged, add-on products bought with the loan (such as GAP or warranties), the interest rate, or the loan being sold or transferred.
Problems at the end of the loan or lease: Problems when the vehicle loan or lease ends: paying it off, getting the title after payoff, selling or giving up the vehicle, lease-end mileage or damage fees, early termination, refinancing, buying or extending the lease.
Struggling to pay your loan: The borrower cannot keep up with payments: a request to lower payments was denied, the lender is trying to repossess or disable the vehicle, a balance remains after repossession and sale, or bankruptcy.
Getting a loan or lease: Problems obtaining vehicle financing: a fraudulent loan, credit denial, misleading advertising, terms changed mid-deal or after closing, high-pressure sales, paperwork, add-on products or a trade-in.
Dealing with your lender or servicer: Problems with how the student loan servicer handles the account: bad information, how payments are handled, fees, customer service, balance or loan terms information, or repeated calls.
Struggling to repay your loan: The borrower cannot afford payments and cannot get relief: flexible or income-driven repayment options, lowering monthly payments, or temporarily delaying payments through deferment or forbearance.
Getting a loan: Problems when taking out a student loan: a fraudulent loan, misleading advertising, being denied, the interest rate, qualifying for a better loan than offered, or signing the paperwork.
Problem with a purchase shown on your st: A charge on the statement the consumer disputes: unauthorized or fraudulent charges, billing errors, items not received, or refunds and chargebacks.
Fees or interest: Disputes about interest rates, APR increases, late fees, annual fees or other charges applied to the credit card account.
Getting a credit card: Problems getting a card: a card opened through identity theft or fraud, a card sent without applying, the application denied or delayed, or trouble getting a working replacement card.
Problem when making payments: Problems paying the card bill: payments not credited, delayed or misapplied, autopay or payment processing errors, or never receiving the bill or not knowing a payment was due.
Closing your account: The issuer closed the card account, or the consumer had trouble closing it, including effects on credit or remaining balances and rewards.
Advertising and marketing, including pro: The card's advertised or promotional terms were not received (promotional rates, sign-up bonuses, rewards, balance transfer offers), or the advertising was confusing or misleading.
Trouble using your card: The card could not be used as expected: purchases declined or the card blocked, the issuer will not raise or lower the credit limit, or the account was sold or transferred.
Struggling to pay your bill: The cardholder cannot keep up with payments: the issuer will not work with them during financial hardship, will not lower monthly payments, or the cardholder filed for bankruptcy.
